opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the next generation of AI labs will look quite different from the ones we've seen over the past decade.

The first wave of labs was built around a fairly clear recipe: gather a lot of compute, a lot of data, and a strong research team, then scale. That worked remarkably well. But we're reaching a point where scaling alone isn't the whole story. Easily available high-quality data is getting scarcer, compute is expensive, and the gains increasingly come from smarter choices about what to train on, how to train, and how models interact with the world after training.

So I think the next labs will be more focused. Instead of trying to be everything to everyone, many will pick a specific problem, like scientific discovery, reasoning, agents that do real work, or particular domains like biology or materials, and build the whole stack around it. That includes the data pipelines, the evaluation methods, and often the feedback loops with the real world. In many of these areas the bottleneck isn't model size. It's having the right signal to learn from.

I also think they'll be smaller and more efficient. A small team with a clear thesis and good taste can now do things that took hundreds of people a few years ago, partly because the tools are better and partly because the models themselves can speed up research. AI helping to build AI, through writing code, running experiments, and generating and filtering data, is going to change how a lab operates day to day.

Another shift is the line between research and product getting blurrier. The best signal often comes from deployment, from real users and real tasks. So I expect labs to be much closer to their applications, iterating quickly on what actually works rather than optimizing benchmarks in isolation.

Finally, data is going to be a core competency rather than an afterthought. Synthetic data, curation, and learning from interaction will separate labs from one another more than architecture will. Architectures tend to converge. How you build and refine your data is where much of the lasting advantage will come from.

So overall: more specialized, more efficient, closer to the real world, and much more deliberate about data. It's an exciting time to be building one.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will help labs write code, run experiments, and generate data, but it does not raise the possibility that AI will run the labs themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the next generation of labs is going to look less like a research institute and more like a product company that happens to do frontier research, and that shift changes almost everything about how they're organized.

The first generation, the OpenAI and DeepMind of ten years ago, were built around the question "can we make this work at all?" You had large, relatively open research cultures, a lot of publishing, and compute was expensive but not yet the single dominant constraint. The current generation is defined by scale: whoever can line up the most compute and the best data pipeline tends to win, and that pushed labs toward secrecy, enormous capital raises, and very tight coupling with cloud providers.

What I expect next is a kind of fragmentation. The pretraining frontier is going to consolidate into a handful of players who can afford gigawatt-scale clusters, and honestly that part of the industry will start to look like semiconductor fabs or telecom: a few very capital-intensive firms with long planning horizons. But on top of that, I think you'll see a lot of smaller labs that don't train base models at all. They take an open or licensed frontier model and spend their entire effort on post-training, on environments, on domain-specific data, on the agentic scaffolding that makes a model actually useful for, say, drug discovery or chip design or legal work. Those labs will be twenty to a hundred people, not a thousand, and their moat will be the data and the feedback loops they build in a specific vertical rather than raw compute.

The other big change is that the unit of research is shifting from the model to the system. Five years ago a lab's output was a checkpoint. Now it's a model plus tools plus memory plus some notion of how it operates over hours or days. So the people you need look different. You still need the people who understand optimization and architecture deeply, but you also need people who think like operating systems engineers and people who think like product designers, and you need them in the same room, because the model's capabilities and how it's deployed are now co-designed.

And I'd add one thing about culture. The early labs attracted people who wanted to work on the hardest open problem in computer science. The next generation is going to have to compete on something else, because a lot of the "does it work" questions have been answered. I think the labs that do well will be the ones with a clear thesis about what the technology is for, and who are willing to be opinionated about safety and about what they won't build. That's partly ethical, but it's also practical. Talent is going to go where people feel the mission is coherent, and increasingly the regulators and the enterprise customers will care about that too.

So, to summarize: a few very large infrastructure players at the bottom, a lot of focused vertical labs on top, systems rather than models as the thing being built, and culture and mission as a real competitive factor rather than a slide in the pitch deck.

r001.rationale: The response describes labs as product companies, infrastructure players, and focused vertical teams, but never suggests that the next generation of labs will be run by AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the next generation of AI labs will probably take a few different forms. You’ll still have large labs where a lot of the work depends on substantial compute and infrastructure. But I also think there’s room for smaller teams that have a very specific research thesis and can test it quickly.

The interesting question is: what lets a lab learn faster? Compute is part of that, but so are the quality of your experiments, how you evaluate progress, and how easily people can share ideas. A small team can be very effective if it’s asking the right questions and getting clear feedback.

I’d also expect AI itself to become a bigger part of the research process—helping write code, analyze results, and propose experiments. That could let researchers explore more ideas. But deciding which questions matter, and whether a result actually supports your hypothesis, will still be essential.

So I don’t think there’s one organizational model that wins. I’d expect a mix of large, broad labs and smaller, focused labs, with more of the routine research work automated.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may help with research tasks and automate routine work, but it does not suggest that AI labs might be run entirely by AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next generation of AI labs will probably look less like a single team training one big model and more like an organization running a continuous loop between research and real-world use. You build a model, see where it struggles on meaningful tasks, and use that feedback to decide what to work on next.

There’s room for different kinds of labs. Some will focus on pushing the frontier, which requires a lot of compute and infrastructure. Others may make progress through better training methods, better data, or a very focused understanding of a particular problem. I wouldn’t assume that every important advance has to come from the largest organization.

The interesting question is how much of the research process AI itself can help with. As models become more useful for writing code, designing experiments, and analyzing results, a small team could do substantially more. But then the bottleneck shifts toward judgment: What experiments are worth running? How do you know a result is meaningful? What are you actually trying to build? I think the strongest labs will be very good at answering those questions.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may help with coding, experiment design, and analysis, but does not raise the possibility that all next-generation AI labs will be run by AI.
